consensus_summary: Across the blind responses, the Ancient of Days is the eternal God (most often God the Father) as sovereign enthroned Judge in Daniel 7; white-haired antiquity signifies pre-existence, wisdom, and judicial authority, with a secondary common alternative identifying the figure with Christ via Revelation 1 imagery.
book_summary: The book glosses Ancient of Days as the venerable One at the origin and advancement of days: one advanced in days who, in Daniel’s calendar vision, sits at the head of the cycle—the day from which month, year, and age advance—explicitly against the common teaching of mere eternal antiquity with no calendar office.
consensus_core_identification: God (typically the Father) as the eternal sovereign Judge of Daniel 7.
book_core_identification: The venerable divine One seated at the head/origin of the day–month–year–age cycle in Daniel’s calendar vision.
boundary_disagreement: Consensus treats antiquity as eternity/pre-existence and judicial kingship without a calendar office; the book assigns a specific calendar-head office (origin and advancement of days) and rejects the ‘no calendar office’ framing.
material_contradiction: None on the basic referent (the Daniel 7 divine enthroned figure remains God); the disagreement is over the title’s symbolic office and precision, not replacement by a non-divine or different person.
rationale: Both readings point to the same Daniel 7 figure as divine; the book preserves that general category while materially narrowing and re-specifying the meaning of attiq yomin from ‘eternal Judge’ to ‘head of the calendar cycle,’ which the book’s own common-view note marks as a departure. This is boundary/precision change (REFINED / BOOK_NARROWS / PARTIAL_RECLASSIFICATION), not core replacement (not DIVERGENT) and not absent from the consensus orbit (not NOVEL).
strongest_objection: The printed texts (Dan 7; Ps 93:2; Isa 43:13) support eternal enthronement and priority ‘before the day,’ but do not by themselves establish a technical calendar-cycle office; mainstream consensus uniformly lacks that office and the book’s contrast with ‘commonly taught’ may over-read the idiom.
